rationale: The batch was built target-first: I enumerated the 16-item menu and deliberately paired targets that need zero, one, or two bits of look-back so the batch does not only probe the easy 'stateless-exact vs one-bit-exact' boundary but also the messier region where neither class is perfect for either mode. Prevalence p was chosen from a spread of odd, non-round fractions (3/7, 4/9, 1/5, 3/4) plus the two required degenerate corners p=0 and p=1, so the batch cannot be satisfied by a theory that only handles symmetric or textbook-round mode weights. Lambda sweeps in each environment span roughly three orders of magnitude (from 1/100 up to 9) so any predicted flip point, wherever it falls, lands inside at least one environment's tested range. Two environments (constant-target and p-degenerate pairs) are included as explicit sanity controls rather than hidden degenerate cases. No candidate machine outputs or winners were computed or simulated while building this batch; only the target menu, L, p, eta, and lambda choices were selected independently of any knowledge of the prediction team's theory.

environments.note: CUR is exactly stateless-solvable; PREV needs one bit of look-back, so the winner should flip from PERSISTENT_STATE to STATELESS as lambda rises through a mid-range value. Canonical flip probe at balanced mode prevalence.

XOR/XNOR both require x_{t-1}, so no stateless machine is exact in either mode. Tests whether the theory still predicts a class flip when the stateless side is only 'best available' rather than perfect.
Longer sequence (L=4) with asymmetric mode targets and eta=2 to check sensitivity to the overall error-weight scale, not just lambda.

Both targets depend on x_{t-2}, beyond what a single state bit can losslessly carry across two steps. Probes whether the theory's prediction degrades gracefully or breaks when neither class has a perfect solution.
CONTROL: p=0 makes mode 1 (AND2) unscored entirely, so this reduces to a single-mode XOR2 problem. Checks the theory handles the p-degenerate edge correctly rather than only interior p.
CONTROL: complementary to E05. p=1 makes mode 0 (OR2) unscored, isolating NAND (a one-bit-history target) as the sole scored objective.
Negated-polarity pair at an odd, non-round p to prevent the batch from only exercising 'nice' fractions a theory's authors might have anticipated.
CONTROL: both targets are trivially stateless-exact (a constant), so the winner should be STATELESS at every lambda tested. Sanity floor the theory must not contradict.
Skewed prevalence toward mode 0 (MAJ3, needs two-back history) with a cheap-to-expensive lambda sweep spanning nearly three orders of magnitude.
Both targets are in the two-back-history family but paired with each other rather than with a one-bit-history target, at an unusual prevalence 4/9.
High mode-1 prevalence (3/4) pairing two two-back targets, with a wide lambda sweep to locate any flip point near the expensive end.

Mixes a trivially stateless target (CUR) with a hard two-back target (MAJ3) in the same environment at balanced prevalence, with a very cheap lambda included to confirm PERSISTENT_STATE can still win when state is nearly free.
